title: What is the difference between a liveness probe and a readiness probe, and how do you wire Spring Boot Actuator (`/actuator/health/liveness`, `/actuator/health/readiness`) to them?
shortTitle: Liveness probe vs readiness probe, and wiring Spring Boot Actuator health groups to them

s1_definition.profdef: A liveness probe and a readiness probe are two independent health checks Kubernetes runs against a container. The liveness probe answers "is this process still healthy, or is it stuck and should be restarted?" — if it fails repeatedly, Kubernetes kills and recreates the container. The readiness probe answers "is this process ready to receive traffic right now?" — if it fails, Kubernetes removes the Pod from the Service's load-balancing pool but does not restart it. In Spring Boot, Actuator exposes two dedicated endpoints for these, `/actuator/health/liveness` and `/actuator/health/readiness`, which you wire to the Kubernetes probes so the application itself decides when it is alive and when it is ready.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture a teller at National Bank of India. The liveness check is the manager asking "are you conscious and at your desk?" — if the teller has fainted, the manager sends them home and calls a replacement. The readiness check is "are you ready to serve the next customer?" — maybe the teller is awake but still counting the opening cash drawer, so the manager temporarily stops sending customers to that window without firing the teller. Liveness decides whether to replace the teller; readiness decides whether to route customers to them right now.
s1_definition.oneliner: Liveness failing means "restart me, I'm stuck"; readiness failing means "pause traffic to me, I'm busy or not ready yet" — never restart on a condition that is merely temporary.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A liveness probe and a readiness probe are two independent health checks Kubernetes runs against a container. The liveness probe answers "is this process still healthy, or is it stuck and should be restarted?" — if it fails repeatedly, Kubernetes kills and recreates the container. The readiness probe answers "is this process ready to receive traffic right now?" — if it fails, Kubernetes removes the Pod from the Service's load-balancing pool but does not restart it. In Spring Boot, Actuator exposes two dedicated endpoints for these, `/actuator/health/liveness` and `/actuator/health/readiness`, which you wire to the Kubernetes probes so the application itself decides when it is alive and when it is ready.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture a teller at National Bank of India. The liveness check is the manager asking "are you conscious and at your desk?" — if the teller has fainted, the manager sends them home and calls a replacement. The readiness check is "are you ready to serve the next customer?" — maybe the teller is awake but still counting the opening cash drawer, so the manager temporarily stops sending customers to that window without firing the teller. Liveness decides whether to replace the teller; readiness decides whether to route customers to them right now.

**One line to remember:** Liveness failing means "restart me, I'm stuck"; readiness failing means "pause traffic to me, I'm busy or not ready yet" — never restart on a condition that is merely temporary.

sections.s2_technical:
The two probes exist because "the process is running" and "the process can serve requests" are different questions, and conflating them causes outages. The liveness probe guards against a deadlocked or wedged process that is technically alive but will never recover on its own. If the liveness probe fails the configured number of times, Kubernetes concludes the container is unrecoverable and restarts it. The readiness probe guards against sending traffic to a Pod that is not yet able to handle it, either because it is still starting up, or because a dependency it needs is temporarily unavailable. When readiness fails, Kubernetes takes the Pod out of the Service endpoints so no new traffic arrives, but it leaves the Pod running so it can recover and rejoin.

The critical design rule is what each probe is allowed to check. The liveness probe must check only the process's own internal health, such as whether the main thread is responsive. It must never check external dependencies like the database, because if the database has a brief hiccup and the liveness probe checks it, every Pod will fail liveness simultaneously and Kubernetes will restart your entire fleet at once, turning a minor dependency blip into a full outage. The readiness probe, by contrast, may check dependencies, because the correct response to a missing dependency is to stop taking traffic, not to restart. This distinction is the single most important thing to get right.

Spring Boot Actuator supports this directly through health groups and an application-availability concept. When the application runs in a Kubernetes-like environment, Actuator exposes two grouped endpoints. The liveness endpoint reports the LivenessState, which is UP as long as the application's internal state is healthy and the application has not entered a broken state it cannot leave. The readiness endpoint reports the ReadinessState, which is UP when the application has finished starting and is accepting traffic, and REFUSING_TRAFFIC when it is still warming up or deliberately draining. Spring Boot automatically manages these states during startup and graceful shutdown: during shutdown it flips readiness to REFUSING_TRAFFIC first so the load balancer drains it before the process stops.

You enable this by exposing the health endpoint and turning on the probes. In configuration you include health in the exposed endpoints and set the probes to enabled, which makes Spring Boot publish the liveness and readiness groups. You can add your own health indicators to the readiness group, for example a check that a required downstream service is reachable, while deliberately keeping the liveness group limited to internal checks only.

On the Kubernetes side you point each probe at the matching endpoint. The liveness probe performs an HTTP GET on the liveness path, and the readiness probe performs an HTTP GET on the readiness path. You tune the timing carefully: an initial delay or, better, a startup probe to cover slow application boot so the liveness probe does not kill a container that is simply still starting; a period for how often to check; a failure threshold for how many consecutive failures trigger action; and a timeout per check. For a JVM application that can take time to warm up, using a startup probe to gate the liveness probe is the clean way to avoid premature restarts.

The senior-level nuance is the interplay during a rolling update, which ties directly to zero downtime. Kubernetes only shifts traffic to a new Pod once its readiness probe passes, and it only removes an old Pod after draining. If readiness honestly reflects warm-up — connection pools filled, caches primed, dependencies reachable — then a rolling update never routes a customer to a Pod that cannot serve them. If readiness lies and reports UP too early, users see errors during every deploy. So accurate probes are not a nicety; they are the mechanism that makes zero-downtime deployment real.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, the Transfer Service is a Spring Boot application on Kubernetes. It needs correct liveness and readiness behaviour so that deploys are seamless and transient database blips do not restart the whole fleet.

Problem 1 — When a new Transfer Service Pod starts, it must fill its database connection pool and warm a currency-rate cache before it can serve transfers. If Kubernetes routes customers to it the instant the process starts, those first requests fail. This is exactly what the readiness probe solves: the Pod reports not-ready until warm-up finishes, so traffic only arrives when it can actually be served.

Problem 2 — Occasionally the database has a two-second blip. If the liveness probe checked the database, every Pod would fail liveness at once and Kubernetes would restart the entire fleet, turning a two-second blip into a multi-minute outage. This is exactly why the liveness probe must check only internal state, never dependencies.

Problem 3 — During a rolling update, old Pods must drain gracefully so in-flight transfers complete. This is exactly what the readiness state during shutdown solves: the Pod flips to refusing traffic first, the load balancer stops sending new requests, in-flight work finishes, and only then does the process exit.

To make this runnable, we will build a small program that models the two probes. It will contain an `AvailabilityState` holding liveness and readiness flags, a `HealthEndpoints` class exposing a liveness check that looks only at internal state and a readiness check that also considers a simulated database dependency and a warm-up flag, and a `KubeletSimulator` that periodically polls both probes and reacts correctly — restarting on liveness failure and removing from the pool on readiness failure. The demo starts a Pod cold, shows it become ready after warm-up, simulates a database blip to prove liveness stays UP while readiness drops, and finally triggers graceful shutdown.
sections.s4a_structure:
Project structure:

```
transfer-service/
├── pom.xml
├── k8s/
│   └── deployment-with-probes.yml
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/com/bank/transfer/
│   │   │   ├── ProbeDemo.java                     (main class)
│   │   │   ├── health/
│   │   │   │   ├── AvailabilityState.java          (liveness + readiness flags)
│   │   │   │   └── HealthEndpoints.java            (the two probe endpoints)
│   │   │   └── kube/
│   │   │       └── KubeletSimulator.java           (polls and reacts)
│   │   └── resources/
│   │       └── application.yml
│   └── test/
│       └── java/com/bank/transfer/
│           └── health/
│               └── HealthEndpointsTest.java
```

Configuration file (the real Spring Boot wiring):

```yaml
# application.yml
management:
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true          # publish liveness & readiness groups
      group:
        readiness:
          include: readinessState, db, warmup   # readiness MAY check deps
        liveness:
          include: livenessState                 # liveness ONLY internal state
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health
server:
  shutdown: graceful           # drain in-flight requests on SIGTERM
```

The Kubernetes manifest wiring probes to endpoints:

```yaml
# k8s/deployment-with-probes.yml (probe section)
startupProbe:                    # gates liveness until the JVM has booted
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
  failureThreshold: 30
  periodSeconds: 2
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3           # 3 straight failures -> restart container
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 2           # 2 straight failures -> remove from Service
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build and run the model
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/transfer-service-1.0.0.jar

# Check the real endpoints on a running Spring Boot service
curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/health/liveness
curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/health/readiness
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a single Transfer Service Pod that starts cold, warms up, suffers a brief database blip, recovers, and then shuts down gracefully, with the kubelet polling both probes at each phase.

Step 1: At startup the process is alive but not warmed up. The liveness endpoint checks only internal state and reports UP because nothing is broken. The readiness endpoint reports not ready because warm-up has not finished. The kubelet sees liveness UP so it does not restart, and readiness down so the Pod is not added to the Service pool. No customer traffic arrives yet, which is exactly right.

Step 2: Warm-up completes — the connection pool is filled and the cache is primed — so the availability state is marked warmed up. On the next poll, readiness now reports UP. The kubelet adds the Pod to the Service pool, and only now does traffic begin flowing to it.

Step 3: The database suffers a two-second blip, modelled by setting dbReachable to false. The readiness endpoint, which does check dependencies, now reports refusing traffic. The liveness endpoint, which deliberately does not check the database, still reports UP. The kubelet removes the Pod from the Service pool so no new transfers are routed to it, but critically it does not restart the container, because the process itself is fine.

Step 4: The database recovers and dbReachable returns to true. Readiness reports UP again on the next poll, and the kubelet adds the Pod back to the Service pool. The blip caused a brief pause in traffic to this Pod but no restart and no outage, which is the entire point of separating the two probes.

Step 5: Graceful shutdown begins. The application flips to refusing traffic first. Readiness immediately reports refusing traffic, so the kubelet drains the Pod out of the Service pool before the process exits, allowing in-flight transfers to finish. Liveness is irrelevant at this point because the Pod is being removed deliberately.

Final output:

```text
Oct 25, 2026 2:02:14 AM com.bank.transfer.kube.KubeletSimulator poll
WARNING: startup: readiness DOWN -> REMOVE from Service pool (no restart)
INFO: after-warmup: readiness UP -> ADD to Service pool (traffic flows)
WARNING: db-blip: readiness DOWN -> REMOVE from Service pool (no restart)
INFO: db-recovered: readiness UP -> ADD to Service pool (traffic flows)
WARNING: draining: readiness DOWN -> REMOVE from Service pool (no restart)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  kubelet polls two independent probes
    │
    ├─ GET /actuator/health/liveness ──→ checks ONLY internal state
    │     UP  → leave running
    │     DOWN×3 → RESTART container
    │
    └─ GET /actuator/health/readiness ─→ checks warm-up + DB + draining
          UP  → ADD Pod to Service endpoints (traffic flows)
          DOWN → REMOVE Pod from Service endpoints (NO restart)

  Timeline for one Pod:
    startup        liveness UP,  readiness DOWN   → not in pool (warming up)
    after-warmup   liveness UP,  readiness UP     → in pool, serving
    db-blip 2s     liveness UP,  readiness DOWN   → out of pool, NOT restarted
    db-recovered   liveness UP,  readiness UP     → back in pool
    draining       liveness UP,  readiness DOWN   → drained, then exit
```

```text
  ═══ LLD — Health Probe Design ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  State Pattern: AvailabilityState holds liveness/readiness flags  │

  ┌──────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │  KubeletSimulator     │───────▶│  HealthEndpoints         │
  │ - livenessFailures    │ polls  │ + liveness(): boolean    │ internal only
  │ - inServicePool       │        │ + readiness(): boolean   │ deps + warmup
  │ + poll(phase)         │        └────────────┬─────────────┘
  └──────────────────────┘                      │ reads
                                                 ▼
                                   ┌──────────────────────────┐
                                   │  AvailabilityState        │
                                   │ - livenessBroken          │
                                   │ - warmedUp                │
                                   │ - dbReachable             │
                                   │ - refusingTraffic         │
                                   └──────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: ReadinessState ──────────────────────────
  [starting: REFUSING] --warmup done--> [UP] --dep down--> [REFUSING]
        ▲                                 │ --shutdown-->  [REFUSING] → exit
        └────────── dep recovered ────────┘

  ── Call Chain (per poll) ───────────────────────────────
  1. KubeletSimulator.poll(phase)
  2.   → HealthEndpoints.liveness() → AvailabilityState.isLivenessBroken()
  3.   → HealthEndpoints.readiness() → warmedUp && dbReachable && !refusing
  4.   → if !live ×3 → RESTART ; if !ready → REMOVE from pool
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A liveness probe and a readiness probe answer two different questions, and the whole art is keeping them separate. The liveness probe asks "is this process healthy, or is it wedged and should be restarted?" If it fails the configured number of times, Kubernetes kills and recreates the container. The readiness probe asks "is this Pod able to serve traffic right now?" If it fails, Kubernetes removes the Pod from the Service's load-balancing pool but leaves it running so it can recover and rejoin. Restarting is the response to liveness failure; pausing traffic is the response to readiness failure.

The most important rule is what each probe may check. The liveness probe must check only the process's own internal state and must never check external dependencies like the database. If liveness checked the database and the database had a brief hiccup, every Pod would fail liveness at the same instant and Kubernetes would restart the entire fleet, turning a two-second blip into a full outage. The readiness probe, on the other hand, may check dependencies, because the correct response to a missing dependency is to stop taking traffic, not to restart.

In Spring Boot I wire this with Actuator's health groups and application availability. I enable the probes so Actuator publishes two grouped endpoints: the liveness group includes only the internal liveness state, and the readiness group includes the readiness state plus dependency and warm-up indicators. On the Kubernetes side, the liveness probe does an HTTP GET on the liveness path and the readiness probe on the readiness path, and I use a startup probe to cover the JVM's slow boot so liveness never kills a container that is merely still starting. Spring Boot also manages these states automatically during graceful shutdown: it flips readiness to refusing-traffic first so the load balancer drains the Pod before the process exits.

At National Bank of India this separation is what made our deploys invisible to customers. When a new Transfer Service Pod started, it reported not-ready until its connection pool was filled and its currency-rate cache was primed, so Kubernetes only routed customers to it once it could truly serve them. When the database had an occasional blip, readiness dropped and the Pod was pulled from the pool for a moment, but liveness stayed up so nothing was restarted, and the Pod rejoined the instant the database recovered. And during rolling updates, old Pods drained gracefully so in-flight transfers completed. Accurate probes were not a nicety; they were the exact mechanism that turned the objective of zero-downtime deployment into reality.
